Intend
ĭn-tĕnd'
v. (to purpose, to mean to do; the settled aim of the will before the act)
Latin intendere, to stretch toward, from in-, toward, and tendere, to stretch — the mind stretched out after an object. The Greek mello means to be about to do a thing.

Biblical Definition

Intention is what a man is stretching toward, and Scripture treats it as a real thing that can be examined and judged. When the western tribes built their altar, the rest of Israel armed for war until the purpose was explained, and then “the children of Israel blessed God, and did not intend to go up against them in battle” (Jos 22:33) — a war was stopped by discovering an intention. Oded warns Israel that they are about to compound a national sin: “ye intend to add more to our sins and to our trespass” (2Ch 28:13). The Sanhedrin accuses the apostles of an intention: “ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us” (Act 5:28), and Gamaliel answers with the soberest counsel in the chapter: “take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men” (Act 5:35). The Lord Jesus makes intention the point of a parable about counting: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28). And James sets the boundary that keeps intending from becoming boasting: “For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that” (Jas 4:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to intend as to stretch or extend, and hence to design, to purpose, to fix the mind upon as a thing to be done or accomplished.

expand to see more

INTEND, v.t. [L. intendo; in and tendo, to tend, to stretch.] To stretch; to extend.

2. To design; to purpose; to fix the mind on as a thing to be done or accomplished.

Intending to build a tower. Luke xiv.

3. To regard; to fix the mind on; to attend.

Key Scripture

Jos 22:33 — "And the thing pleased the children of Israel; and the children of Israel blessed God, and did not intend to go up against them in battle, to destroy the land wherein the children of Reuben and Gad dwelt."

Act 5:35 — "And said unto them, Ye men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men."

Luk 14:28 — "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?"

Jas 4:15 — "For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that."

Modern Corruption

Good intentions have become a defence against the judgment of actions, though Scripture judges the intention and the act together and never lets one excuse the other.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors run about intention and both are common. The first says that intention is everything: a man who meant well cannot be blamed for what he did, and to raise the outcome is to be unkind. Scripture will not have it. Uzzah meant to steady the ark and died; the law provided a city of refuge for the man who killed unawares, which is precisely an acknowledgment that a death has happened even where the intent was absent. Meaning well does not undo a wrong, though it changes how the wrong is dealt with. The second error says intention is nothing, and only results are moral. Scripture will not have that either: the Lord names the look as adultery and the hatred as murder, because the will has already stretched toward the thing. A man is answerable for what he aimed at and for what he did.

The pastoral use of the word is at Luke 14:28. The Lord makes intending to build a tower the picture of intending to follow Him, and the whole force of the parable is that an intention untested by counting is worthless. Our own religious culture is full of intention treated as achievement — the resolution announced, the commitment made publicly, the plan for discipleship laid out in detail — and it is precisely what the Lord tells men not to do until they have sat down and reckoned. Gamaliel's warning is the other side of it. Take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do: an intention is a thing a man can be warned off before he has moved a hand, because God sees it already. James supplies the only safe way to hold any intention at all, which is under the will of God — not as a pious tag on the end of a plan, but as an honest acknowledgment that the man who intends does not own tomorrow.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mello (G3195), to be about to do; boulomai (G1014), to will or purpose deliberately; Hebrew zamam (H2161), to purpose or devise.

expand to see more

Greek mello (G3195) — to be about to, to intend; what the council intended to do, and what a man intends to build; Acts 5:35, Luke 14:28.

Greek boulomai (G1014) — to will, to purpose after deliberation; used of God's determinate purpose and of a man's settled intent; Hebrews 6:17, James 4:4.

Hebrew zamam (H2161) — to purpose, to devise; the LORD hath done that which he had devised; Lamentations 2:17.

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, to intend; ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good; Genesis 50:20.

Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting forth, a purpose; the purpose of God according to election; Romans 9:11, Ephesians 1:11.

Usage

"“Did not intend to go up against them in battle” — a war stopped by an intention discovered."

"“Take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do” — a man warned off before his hand moves."

"“Intending to build a tower” — the intention that must be counted before it is announced."
